summary.text: Take \(N=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot4409\cdot458009\), where the three prime-power factors are coprime. Multiplicativity and the prime-power divisor-sum formulas give \(\sigma(N)=66183576284700\) and \(\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)=132367152569399\), so \(a(N)=2\sigma(N)-\sum_{d\mid N}\sigma(d)=1\), although \(N\ne1,12\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\sigma(m)=\sum_{e\mid m}e\) denote the sum of the positive divisors of \(m\). The deficiency used in the definition of A296075 is
\[
\operatorname{def}(m)=2m-\sigma(m),
\]
so the sequence in question is
\[
a(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr).
\]
We will exhibit a positive integer other than \(1\) and \(12\) for which this sum is \(1\).

The counterexample is
\[
N=33085221781504=2^{14}\cdot 4409\cdot 458009.
\]
The two odd factors \(4409\) and \(458009\) are prime. For completeness, their primality can be established by the following short Lucas primality certificates.

We use the standard Lucas criterion: if \(m>1\), the complete prime factorization of \(m-1\) is known, and there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m
\]
and, for every prime \(r\mid m-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(m-1)/r}-1,m\bigr)=1,
\]
then \(m\) is prime. The criterion follows because these conditions force the multiplicative order of \(b\), modulo every possible prime divisor of \(m\), to contain every prime-power factor of \(m-1\); consequently a prime divisor of \(m\) must be at least \(m\), which is possible only when \(m\) itself is prime.

The elementary primes \(2,3,5\) start the certificates. Repeated squaring gives the following data; in every displayed row the chosen base also satisfies \(b^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m\). The listed residues are \(b^{(m-1)/r}\pmod m\), and in each case the gcd of one less than that residue with \(m\) is \(1\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
m& m-1&b& r:\ b^{(m-1)/r}\pmod m\\ \hline
7&2\cdot3&3&2:6,\quad 3:2\\
19&2\cdot3^2&2&2:18,\quad 3:7\\
29&2^2\cdot7&2&2:28,\quad 7:16\\
229&2^2\cdot3\cdot19&6&2:228,\quad 3:134,\quad 19:165\\
57251&2\cdot5^3\cdot229&2&2:57250,\quad 5:55371,\quad 229:48088\\
4409&2^3\cdot19\cdot29&3&2:4408,\quad 19:209,\quad 29:3965\\
458009&2^3\cdot57251&3&2:458008,\quad 57251:6561.
\end{array}
\]

For example, in the row for \(4409\), the assertions are
\[
3^{4408}\equiv1\pmod{4409},
\]
while
\[
3^{2204}\equiv4408,
\quad 3^{232}\equiv209,
\quad 3^{152}\equiv3965\pmod{4409},
\]
and each of \(4408-1\), \(209-1\), and \(3965-1\) is relatively prime to \(4409\). The other rows have exactly the same interpretation. Direct Euclidean-algorithm calculations give all the stated gcds as \(1\). Applying the Lucas criterion upward through the rows proves successively that \(7,19,29,229,57251,4409\), and \(458009\) are prime. Thus the displayed factorization of \(N\) is a factorization into pairwise coprime prime powers. Its numerical value follows from
\[
2^{14}=16384,
\qquad 16384\cdot4409=72237056,
\]
and
\[
72237056\cdot458009=33085221781504.
\]

We now reduce the sum defining \(a(n)\). Define
\[
T(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d).
\]
Then, simply separating the two terms in the deficiency sum,
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(n)
&=\sum_{d\mid n}\bigl(2d-\sigma(d)\bigr)\\
&=2\sum_{d\mid n}d-\sum_{d\mid n}\sigma(d)\\
&=2\sigma(n)-T(n).
\end{aligned}
\]

Both \(\sigma\) and \(T\) are multiplicative on coprime arguments. Indeed, if \(x\) and \(y\) are coprime, every divisor of \(xy\) is uniquely of the form \(uv\), where \(u\mid x\) and \(v\mid y\), and \(u,v\) are themselves coprime. This gives
\[
\sigma(xy)
 =\sum_{u\mid x}\sum_{v\mid y}uv
 =\left(\sum_{u\mid x}u\right)
  \left(\sum_{v\mid y}v\right)
 =\sigma(x)\sigma(y).
\]
Using this and the same unique decomposition of divisors,
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(xy)
 &=\sum_{u\mid x}\sum_{v\mid y}\sigma(uv)\\
 &=\sum_{u\mid x}\sum_{v\mid y}\sigma(u)\sigma(v)\\
 &=T(x)T(y).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus both quantities needed for \(a(N)\) can be calculated separately on the three prime-power factors of \(N\).

For a prime \(p\) and an exponent \(e\geq0\),
\[
\sigma(p^e)=1+p+\cdots+p^e.
\]
Moreover, since the divisors of \(p^e\) are \(1,p,\ldots,p^e\),
\[
T(p^e)=\sum_{j=0}^{e}\sigma(p^j)
       =\sum_{j=0}^{e}\sum_{k=0}^{j}p^k.
\]
In particular,
\[
\sigma(2^{14})=1+2+\cdots+2^{14}=2^{15}-1=32767.
\]
Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(2^{14})
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}(1+2+\cdots+2^j)\\
 &=\sum_{j=0}^{14}(2^{j+1}-1)\\
 &=(2+4+\cdots+2^{15})-15\\
 &=65534-15\\
 &=65519.
\end{aligned}
\]

For a prime occurring to the first power, the corresponding formulas reduce to
\[
\sigma(p)=p+1,
\qquad
T(p)=\sigma(1)+\sigma(p)=1+(p+1)=p+2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
q&\sigma(q)&T(q)\\ \hline
4409&4410&4411\\
458009&458010&458011.
\end{array}
\]

Multiplicativity now yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma(N)
 &=\sigma(2^{14})\sigma(4409)\sigma(458009)\\
 &=32767\cdot4410\cdot458010.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first two factors multiply to
\[
32767\cdot4410=144502470,
\]
and hence
\[
\sigma(N)=144502470\cdot458010=66183576284700.
\]
Likewise,
\[
\begin{aligned}
T(N)
 &=T(2^{14})T(4409)T(458009)\\
 &=65519\cdot4411\cdot458011.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here
\[
65519\cdot4411=289004309,
\]
so
\[
T(N)=289004309\cdot458011=132367152569399.
\]
Substituting these two values into \(a(N)=2\sigma(N)-T(N)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(N)
 &=2\cdot66183576284700-132367152569399\\
 &=132367152569400-132367152569399\\
 &=1.
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally,
\[
N=33085221781504>12,
\]
so \(N\) is neither \(1\) nor \(12\). We have therefore found a positive integer \(N\notin\{1,12\}\) for which \(a(N)=1\). This directly disproves the proposed biconditional that, for every positive integer \(n\), \(a(n)=1\) if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n=12\).
